To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the cost of seniors' prescription drug coverage is rising, but that the cost of drugs per senior is falling.

the cost of prescription drugs to seniors in BC increased by over 100% in 2001 dollars over the period 1991 to 2001, that this was due in part to an aging population, in part to an increased rate of utilization, and in part to a shift in the type of therapies and products selected.
the population of seniors and their utilization of prescription drugs increased, but this was only a partial explanation for the observed inflation in the cost of prescription drugs for seniors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the nature and importance of different cost driving trends in a prescription drug market, and how these trends are affected by public drug policy.
the relative contribution of the population, utilization, mix and price of products in explaining the observed increase in prescription drug costs for the seniors population of British Columbia.
the relative importance of different drivers of drug expenditure inflation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
seniors' prescription drug cost-driving trends were dominated by increases in the number of seniors, and in the rate at which seniors used drugs.
the inflation in drug expenditures for BC seniors was driven by the increased utilization and the mix of therapies used, and the selection of products with higher prices.
the cost of prescription drugs to the seniors' population in BC has risen due to the increased use of more expensive drugs and therapies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the most important cost drivers for prescription drug costs for seniors are the utilization and mix of therapies, with generic substitution being the most important factor for price inflation.

, for BC seniors, increases in the population of users, and in the rate at which seniors used therapies, were the primary drivers of drug cost inflation, and that the price inflation of products selected was the primary driver of cost increases for the therapies selected.

the cost inflation in prescription drug expenditures for the seniors population was largely due to increased utilization of therapies and increased costs for therapies, and not due to price inflation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, for the population of BC seniors, the main drivers of prescription drug cost inflation are the utilization of therapies and the choice of product.
cost-drivers in the prescription drug sector are not all of the same magnitude, and that the most cost-effective policy interventions are those that target cost-drivers that are most important.
the cost of prescription drugs for seniors in British Columbia was driven by the utilization of more expensive therapies and the selection of higher cost products.
